questions.q: In 2 Thessalonians 3:10, Paul explicitly outlines a principle regarding the dignity of labor. He commands: "If anyone is not willing to work, let him not ______."
questions.explain: Paul condemned idleness among believers, stating firmly: "For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat."

questions.q: According to Paul's teaching in Colossians 3:23, whatever work a person does, they should work heartily, as for ______ and not for men.
questions.explain: Paul dignifies all honest labor by elevating its purpose: "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward."

questions.q: In Romans 13:1-7, what profound reason does Paul give for why every Christian must be subject to the governing authorities?
options: Because the governing authorities always make perfect laws
Because there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God
Because it is the only way to avoid paying taxes
Because authorities will eventually become Christians
questions.explain: Paul teaches obedience to constituted authority by pointing to God's sovereignty: "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God."

questions.q: In Paul's letter to the Ephesians (Eph 6:5-8), he instructs servants to obey their earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as they would obey ________.
questions.explain: Ephesians 6:5 states: "Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ."

questions.q: In Romans 13:8-10, Paul summarizes the commandments such as "You shall not commit adultery" and "You shall not steal" into one phrase. What is this phrase?
options: "You shall honor the temple of the Lord."
"You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
questions.explain: Paul states that "he who loves another has fulfilled the law," summarizing it with the commandment, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."

questions.q: When Paul arrived in Jerusalem (Acts 21), a violent riot broke out in the temple and he was dragged out. What false accusation sparked this mob against him?
options: That he was planning to assassinate the High Priest
That he brought Greeks into the temple and defiled the holy place
That he had stolen gold from the temple treasury
That he claimed to be the Messiah
questions.explain: Jews from Asia stirred up the crowd, crying out, "...he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place." They wrongly assumed he brought Trophimus the Ephesian inside.

questions.q: During Paul's trial before the Sanhedrin (Acts 23:6), he cleverly divided the council by crying out that he was on trial with respect to the hope of ________.
options: the destruction of the Roman Empire
questions.explain: Perceiving that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, Paul cried out, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee... It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial." This caused a violent dispute since Sadducees did not believe in resurrection.

questions.q: Following Paul's appearance before the Jewish Council, a group of more than forty Jews formed a conspiracy. What did they bind themselves under an oath to do? (Acts 23:12-14)
options: To neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul
To leave Jerusalem and never return
To fast for forty days in the wilderness until Paul was released
To offer continuous sacrifices until Paul was executed by Rome
questions.explain: They made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. This plot was foiled when Paul's nephew overheard them and warned the Roman tribune.

questions.q: After being secretly moved from Jerusalem under heavy military guard to Caesarea, who was the first Roman governor that heard Paul's case?
questions.explain: Paul was brought by night to Caesarea and presented to **Felix** the governor (Acts 23:33). Felix kept Paul in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.

questions.q: When Porcius Festus succeeded Felix, he wanted to do the Jews a favor and suggested Paul be tried in Jerusalem. How did Paul dramatically escape this trap? (Acts 25:10-11)
options: He invoked his rights as a Roman citizen and appealed to Caesar.
He proved his absolute innocence from the Scriptures.
He requested a trial by combat against the High Priest.
questions.explain: As a Roman citizen, Paul had the right to demand trial in Rome. He stated, "I am standing before Caesar's tribunal... I appeal to Caesar." Festus replied, "To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go."
questions.exam: BECE CRS: Christian Religious Studies: New Testament Part 1 (Paper 2)

questions.q: While Paul was waiting in Caesarea to be sent to Rome, Festus invited a visiting royal dignitary to hear Paul speak. Who was this royal guest?
questions.explain: Acts 25:13 states: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus." Paul later gave his famous defense before King Agrippa (Acts 26).
